1 Safety
Read this manual before installing, operating or servicing the pump. Work on the pump only when you
are trained for the task and the pump is isolated as your site's procedures require.
+ Isolate the motor electrically and lock it out before any work on the pump.
+ Release the pressure in the casing and the seal-water line before opening any connection.
+ Wear safety glasses and gloves when handling the mechanical seal. The seal faces are brittle and
their edges are sharp.
+ Never run the pump dry or against a closed suction valve.
+ Lift the pump only by the lifting lugs on the baseplate, never by the motor eyebolt.
2 Description
The CP-200 is a single-stage, end-suction centrifugal pump with a closed impeller, designed for clean or
slightly contaminated water at up to 90 °C. The pump and its motor sit on a common baseplate and are
joined by a flexible spacer coupling, so the rotating assembly can be removed without disturbing the
pipework.
The shaft is sealed by a cartridge mechanical seal flushed with clean seal water from an external
supply. Two grease-lubricated ball bearings in the bearing housing carry the shaft. A controller on the
pump skid monitors the motor, the bearing temperatures and the seal-water pressure and trips the
pump when a limit is exceeded.

4.1 Foundation and baseplate
Set the baseplate on a concrete foundation at least 1.5 times the weight of the pump and motor: Level
the baseplate to within 0.2 mm per meter with shims next to the anchor bolts, then grout it. Check the
coupling alignment after the grout has cured, because tightening the anchor bolts distorts an ungrouted
baseplate.
4.2 Pipework
Support the suction and discharge pipes independently of the pump; the pump flanges must carry no
pipe loads. Make the suction pipe at least one size larger than the suction flange and keep it free of high
points where air can collect. Fit a strainer in the suction line during the first weeks of operation and
remove it once the system is clean.
4.3 Seal-water connection
Connect the seal-water supply to the flush connection marked SW on the seal housing. Fit an isolation
valve, a strainer and a pressure gauge in the line. The seal-water pressure must exceed the suction
pressure by at least 1 bar whenever the pump runs.
5 Commissioning
5.1 Checks before the first start
1. Check that the rotating assembly turns freely by hand.
2. Check the coupling alignment and fit the coupling guard.
3. Check that the bearings are greased; pumps leave the factory greased for 4,000 hours.
4. Flush the suction pipe and the seal-water line before connecting them.
5.4 Start-up
Before the first start, and after any work on the seal or the impeller, prime the pump and check the
seal-water supply.
1. Open the suction valve fully. Never throttle the suction side.
2. Vent the casing at the vent plug until water flows without air.
3. Open the seal-water supply and confirm a pressure of 2.0 to 3.0 bar at the seal flush connection.
The seal-water pressure must exceed the suction pressure by at least 1 bar.
4. Open the discharge valve about one quarter.
5. Jog the motor and confirm the direction of rotation against the arrow on the bearing housing.
6. Start the pump, then open the discharge valve slowly to the duty point within two minutes. Running
against a closed discharge valve for longer overheats the liquid in the casing.
During the first hour, check that the bearing temperatures stay below 80 °C and listen for cavitation
noise.
5.5 Shutdown
1. Close the discharge valve slowly.
2. Stop the motor.
3. Close the seal-water supply only after the pump has stopped, and only if the pump will stay stopped.
4. Drain the casing if the pump may be exposed to frost.

6 Assembly and disassembly
6.1 Removing the rotating assembly
1. Isolate and drain the pump, then remove the coupling guard and the coupling spacer.
2. Undo the casing bolts and pull the rotating assembly back with the bearing housing.
3. Mark the position of the impeller nut before loosening it.
6.2 Impeller clearance
Set the clearance between the impeller and the casing wear ring to 0.3 to 0.5 mm. Replace the wear
ring when the clearance exceeds 1.0 mm.
6.3 Flange bolt torque
Table 6-2 gives the tightening torque for the CP-200 flange bolts. The values apply to bolts of property
class 8.8, lightly oiled, with the spiral-wound gaskets supplied with the pump.
Bolt size Torque
M10 49 N·m
M12 85 N·m
M16 210 N·m
Tighten the M12 flange bolts (property class 8.8, lightly oiled) to 85 N·m. Apply the torque in a cross
pattern in three passes: 30 N·m, 60 N·m, then 85 N·m. Re-check the torque after the first 24 hours of
operation.
Don't reuse spiral-wound gaskets. A gasket that has been compressed once won't seal at the specified
torque.
6.4 Seal housing bolts
Tighten the four seal housing bolts to 45 N·m. Fit the seal housing before the bearing housing is bolted
back to the casing, so that the seal can be centered on the shaft.
7 Maintenance
7.1 Routine checks
+ Daily: listen for unusual noise and check the seal-water pressure at the gauge.
» Weekly: check the seal for leaks; a few drops an hour are normal while the seal runs in.
* Monthly: check the bearing temperatures and the motor current.
7.2 Service intervals
Inspect the mechanical seal and the bearings every 2,000 operating hours or six months, whichever
comes first. Replace mechanical seal PN-4471-B every 8,000 operating hours.

1 Using this guide

detect. Each code's section says what the code means, when the controller raises it, the likely causes in the

hydraulics and the seal, and E-3 the controller and its sensors.
Work through the causes in order. If you clear a code and it returns within an hour, stop and raise a work
order instead of resetting it again.

Causes, most likely first:
1. The pump runs far to the right of its curve because the discharge valve is open too far.
2. The impeller rubs on the wear ring after a bearing failure.
3. The overload relay is set below the motor's rated current.
Find and remove the cause, then reset E-101 at the local panel. The relay resets itself after two minutes.
Error E-102: supply phase missing
Error E-102 means one of the three supply phases is missing. The controller checks the phases at every
start and once a second while the pump runs.
Causes, most likely first:
1. A blown fuse in the motor feeder.
2. A loose terminal in the motor control center.
Have an electrician check the fuses and terminals. E-102 clears itself when all three phases return.
Error E-103: wrong phase sequence
Error E-103 means the supply phase sequence is reversed, so the pump would run backwards. The
controller blocks the start; it never trips a running pump for E-103.
Causes, most likely first:
1. Two supply cables were swapped during electrical work.
Have an electrician swap two phases at the motor terminal box, then confirm the direction of rotation against
the arrow on the bearing housing.
Error E-104: motor winding temperature high
Error E-104 means the motor's winding temperature exceeded 155 °C. The controller trips the pump and
blocks a restart until the windings cool below 120 °C.
Check the motor's cooling fan and fan cover for blockages, and measure the supply voltage on all three
phases; an unbalance of more than 2 percent overheats the windings. Frequent starts also cause E-104: the
CP-200 motor allows no more than six starts per hour.
Reset E-104 at the local panel once the temperature has dropped. Never bypass the thermistor relay.
Error E-105: earth fault
Error E-105 means the controller measured a leakage current to earth above 300 mA. The earth-fault relay
trips the pump at once.
Causes, most likely first:
1. Water in the motor terminal box.
2. Damaged motor cable insulation.
Don't reset E-105 until an electrician has measured the motor's insulation resistance.
Error E-106: supply undervoltage
Error E-106 means the supply voltage stayed below 90 percent of its nominal value for more than 5 seconds.
The pump restarts by itself 30 seconds after the voltage returns, unless automatic restart is disabled.
Causes, most likely first:
1. A weak supply during the start of another large motor.

Error E-201: suction pressure low
Error E-201 means the suction pressure fell below 0.3 bar. The controller warns for 20 seconds before it trips
the pump, to ride through short dips.
Causes, most likely first:
1. The suction valve is partly closed.
2. The suction strainer is blocked.
3. The level in the suction tank is too low.
Open the suction valve fully, clean the suction strainer and check the tank level before resetting E-201.
Error E-202: discharge pressure high
Error E-202 means the discharge pressure rose above 14 bar. The controller trips the pump after 5 seconds
above the limit.
Causes, most likely first:
1. The discharge valve is closed.
2. A check valve downstream is stuck shut.
Open the discharge path, then reset E-202 at the local panel.
Error E-203: dry running
Error E-203 means the dry-running sensor in the casing detected no liquid. The controller trips the pump at
once, because a few seconds of dry running damage the mechanical seal.
Causes, most likely first:
1. The casing wasn't vented after maintenance.
2. The suction tank ran empty.
Vent the casing until water flows without air, then reset E-203. Check the seal for leaks after the restart.
Error E-204: flow low
Error E-204 means the flow fell below 40 m³/h, the pump's minimum continuous flow. The controller warns at
once and trips the pump after 2 minutes of low flow.
Causes, most likely first:
1. The discharge valve is throttled too far.
2. The process no longer needs the pump.
Open the discharge valve or stop the pump, then reset E-204.
Error E-211: seal leakage detected
Error E-211 means the leakage sensor below the seal housing detected liquid. E-211 is a warning; the pump
keeps running.
Causes, most likely first:
1. The mechanical seal is worn.
2. The seal-water connection leaks.
Plan a seal replacement if the leak continues; SOP-FS-014 describes the work.

Error E-217: seal-water pressure low
Error E-217 means seal-water pressure low. The controller trips the pump when seal-water pressure stays
below 1.5 bar for 10 seconds, to protect the mechanical seal. Check that seal-water valve V-114 is open and
that its strainer is clean, then reset the alarm at the local panel.
Common causes, most likely first:
1. Seal-water valve V-114 left closed or partly closed after maintenance.
2. A blocked strainer upstream of V-114 (work instruction WI-FS-031 describes the cleaning).
3. A failed pressure switch PS-31. Compare its reading with the local gauge.
To clear E-217, restore the seal-water pressure to at least 2.0 bar, wait until the alarm light stops flashing,
then press RESET on the local panel. If the alarm returns within an hour, don't restart the pump again; raise
a work order for the seal-water system.
Error E-218: seal-water pressure high
Error E-218 means the seal-water pressure rose above 4.0 bar. E-218 is a warning: high seal-water pressure
wastes water and can push water into the process.
Causes, most likely first:
1. The seal-water pressure regulator failed open.
Set the regulator to 2.5 bar and check that the gauge reads 2.0 to 3.0 bar.
Error E-221: bearing temperature high
Error E-221 means a bearing temperature exceeded 95 °C. The controller warns at 85 °C and trips the pump
at 95 °C.
Causes, most likely first:
1. Too much grease after regreasing.
2. Misalignment between pump and motor.
3. A worn bearing.
Let the bearings cool, check the alignment and the amount of grease, then reset E-221.
Error E-222: vibration high
Error E-222 means the vibration on the bearing housing exceeded 7.1 mm/s RMS. The controller warns at
4.5 mm/s RMS and trips the pump at 7.1 mm/s RMS.
Causes, most likely first:
1. Misalignment after maintenance.
2. Cavitation.
3. Worn bearings or a damaged impeller.
Section 3.1 describes how to find the cause. Don't restart the pump repeatedly after E-222.
Error E-231: liquid temperature high
Error E-231 means the liquid temperature in the casing exceeded 90 °C. The controller trips the pump after
10 seconds above the limit.
Causes, most likely first:
1. The pump ran against a closed discharge valve.
2. The process supplies liquid hotter than the pump's rating.

Error E-320: emergency stop
Error E-320 means an emergency stop button was pressed. The pump stops at once and can't restart until
the button is released and E-320 is reset.

1. Someone pressed an emergency stop button.

Error E-330: clock battery low
Error E-330 means the battery that keeps the controller's clock running is nearly empty. E-330 is a warning;
event logs lose their time stamps once the battery is empty.
Causes, most likely first:
1. The battery is more than five years old.
Replace the CR2032 battery behind the controller's front panel.
3 Mechanical problems
Troubleshooting: excessive vibration
Vibration above 4.5 mm/s RMS on the bearing housing needs investigation; above 7.1 mm/s RMS, stop the
pump.
Likely causes, in the order to check them:
Misalignment between the pump and motor shafts after maintenance. Check the coupling alignment.
•
Cavitation, which sounds like gravel rattling in the casing. It comes from low suction pressure: check that
•
the suction valve is fully open and the suction strainer is clean.
Worn bearings. Bearing noise rises before the vibration does.
•
A loose baseplate or loose foot bolts.
•
A damaged or unbalanced impeller.
•
Cavitation
Cavitation is the collapse of vapor bubbles that form where the pressure at the impeller inlet falls below the
liquid's vapor pressure. It sounds like gravel rattling in the casing and erodes the impeller vanes within
weeks.
Check the suction side first: the suction valve must be fully open, the suction strainer clean and the tank level
above its minimum. If the pump runs far to the right of its curve, throttle the discharge valve back to the duty
point.
Seal leakage
A new mechanical seal may drip for the first few hours while its faces run in. A seal that leaks steadily after
that has worn or damaged faces. The most common causes are dry running, seal-water pressure below 1.5
bar and abrasive particles in the seal water. Replace the seal as SOP-FS-014 describes; don't try to stop a
leak by tightening the gland nuts beyond their torque.
Bearing overheating
Bearings run hottest in the first hours after regreasing, while excess grease is pushed out. A bearing that
stays above 85 °C has too much grease, too little grease, a misaligned coupling or wear. Check the
alignment and the amount of grease before replacing the bearing.

broken wire. The drive stops the motor rather than run at an unknown speed. Check the reference cable and
the device that sends the signal.
